title: RESTING-STATE EEG AS A TOOL TO MONITOR EARLY ELECTROPHYSIOLOGICAL CHANGES DURING
content:
VIRTUAL-073 

Topic: Theme A: β-Amyloid Diseases / A02.r. Therapeutic Targets, Mechanisms for Treatment: AI, Other 

RESTING-STATE EEG AS A TOOL TO MONITOR EARLY ELECTROPHYSIOLOGICAL CHANGES DURING 
LECANEMAB INFUSION 

 

Yumei Liu1, Shaoxia Fan1, Shuhan Fan2, Zian Pei3, Zhifan Zhou2, Xue Shi2, Yi Guo1 
1Shenzhen Bay laboratory, Institute Of Neurological And Psychiatric Disorders, Shenzhen, China, 2Shenzhen People's 
Hospital, Department Of Neurology, shenzhen, China, 3Southern University of Science and Technology, Department Of 
Electronic And Electrical Engineering, shenzhen, China 

Aims: Lecanemab, an anti-amyloid-β monoclonal antibody, slows cognitive decline in Alzheimer’s disease (AD). 
However, its early electrophysiological effects remain unclear. This study examined early resting-state 
electroencephalograms (rsEEG) changes after Lecanemab infusion and assessed whether EEG could predict adverse 
effects. 
Methods: We prospectively collected rsEEG from AD patients before their first Lecanemab infusion, and at days 1, 3, 7, 1 
month, and 3 months post-infusion. Of 32 eligible patients, usable rsEEG was obtained from 25, 20, 18, 22, and 19, 
respectively. Power spectral density and source localization changes were analyzed. 
Results: At baseline, higher theta power correlated with lower MMSE (ρ= -0.38) and MoCA (ρ= -0.42), and higher ADL 
scores (ρ = 0.43). Lower alpha power was linked to higher CDR (ρ= -0.38) and lower MMSE (ρ = 0.38). DTABR(delta + 
theta/alpha +beta) correlated positively with CDR (ρ= 0.41) and ADL (ρ= 0.40), and negatively with MMSE (ρ = -0.43) and 
MoCA (ρ = -0.45). Longitudinally, delta power increased, peaking at day 7 (0.23 ± 0.02 vs. 0.28 ± 0.03; Cohen’s d = 0.89), 
with sources localized to bilateral parietal/temporal and left occipital regions; these changes attenuated by 1 and 3 
months. Delta activity and DTABR correlated with Hypertension-Coronary score (ρ = 0.51) and cognitive decline duration 
(ρ = 0.55). Patients with adverse events (ARIA, infusion reactions, dizziness, allergy) had lower baseline alpha power than 
those without (0.26 ± 0.02 vs. 0.31 ± 0.03; η²p = 0.137). 
Conclusions: Lecanemab induces early electrophysiological changes in AD, marked by increased delta activity and 
DTABR within the first week. RsEEG is sensitive in detecting these alterations and may serve as a noninvasive biomarker 
for both treatment monitoring and predicting adverse events.

title: AI-DRIVEN DIGITAL SPEECH BIOMARKERS DETECT THERAPEUTIC EFFECTS OF TRANSCRANIAL PULSE
content:
VIRTUAL-075 

Topic: Theme A: β-Amyloid Diseases / A02.r. Therapeutic Targets, Mechanisms for Treatment: AI, Other 

AI-DRIVEN DIGITAL SPEECH BIOMARKERS DETECT THERAPEUTIC EFFECTS OF TRANSCRANIAL PULSE 
STIMULATION IN ALZHEIMER’S DISEASE 

 

Daniel Wiechmann1,2, Ali Günes3, Elma Kerz2, Yu Qiao2, Martin Köhne3, Ulrich Sprick3 
1University of Amsterdam, Institute For Logic, Language And Computation, Amsterdam, Germany, 2Exaia Technologies, 
Aachen, Germany, 3Alexius/Josef Krankenhaus, Department Forschung Und Entwicklung, Neurostimulationszentrum, 
Neuss, Germany 

Aims: To develop interpretable AI models using digital biomarkers derived from spontaneous speech to differential 
diagnosis of Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and to individually quantify therapeutic effects of transcranial pulse stimulation 
(TPS) on disease progression. 
Methods: End-to-end automatic classification models were trained using spontaneous speech data from 40 patients with 
clinically diagnosed AD (mean age = 73.8 ± 9.9 years) and 27 healthy controls. Diagnosis was based on current German 
S3 guidelines, including comprehensive neuropsychological assessments (CERAD Plus including MMSE, Stroop-Test) 
and structural MRI. Interpretable AI identified the most discriminative speech features associated with AD pathology. 
Digital speech biomarkers were then used to quantify TPS-related modulation of disease trajectory related to 14 TPS-
treated patients, based on paired recordings acquired 268.7 ± 152.9 days apart. 
Results: Speech biomarkers showed strong correlations with cognitive performance (CERAD r = 0.72; MMSE r = 0.73) 
and outperformed the Stroop test in capturing cognitive impairment. Classification accuracy for AD versus healthy controls 
achieved F1 = 0.81. At the group level, patients receiving TPS showed stable or slightly improved linguistic performance 
throughout the follow-up period, contrasting with the ~3.3-point annual MMSE decline expected in untreated Alzheimer’s 
disease. TPS intervention also revealed pronounced individual variability in t0/t1-speech biomarker trajectories, indicating 
heterogeneous patient responsiveness. Key discriminative speech features identified by the interpretable AI models yield 
mechanistic insights into TPS-related neurophysiological effects. 
Conclusions: This study introduces a novel framework integrating interpretable AI with speech-derived digital biomarkers 
as precision tools for AD diagnosis and monitoring. Findings demonstrate that TPS exerts personalized, measurable 
effects on disease progression, detectable through sensitive speech-based metrics which surpass traditional cognitive 
assessments.

title: EFFECTIVENESS, SAFETY AND BIOMARKER DYNAMICS OF LECANEMAB IN CHINESE ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE

EFFECTIVENESS, SAFETY AND BIOMARKER DYNAMICS OF LECANEMAB IN CHINESE ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE 
POPULATION: A MULTICENTER REAL-WORLD STUDY 

 

Wang Liao1, Qun Yu1, Bin Chen1, Hualin Chen1, Chenyang Wang2, Yang Li2, Ying Yang3, Ziyu She4, Qinggan Zeng5, 
Zengqiang Zhang6, Guihua Li7, Shujun Feng8, Han Lin9, Jipeng Ouyang10, Jun Liu1 
1The Second Affiliated Hospital of Guangzhou Medical University, Guangzhou, China, 2Department of Neurology, 
Department of Pediatric Neurology, Zhujiang Hospital of Southern Medical University, Guangzhou, China, 3Department of 
Neurology, the First Affiliated Hospital of Jinan University Medical College, Guangzhou, China, 4Department of Neurology, 
Zhongshan People's Hospital, Guangdong, Zhongshan, China, 5Department of Neurology, Heyou Hospital, Shunde 
District, Foshan City, Guangdong, China., Foshan, China, 6Hainan Hospital of Chinese PLA Genera Hospital, Sanya, 
China, 7Department of Neurology, The Affiliated Guangdong Second Provincial General Hospital of Jinan University, 
Guangzhou, China, 8Department of Neurology, Guangdong Provincial People’s Hospital, Guangzhou, China, 9Department 
of Neurology, Houjie Hospital of Dongguan, Dongguan, China, 10Department of Neurology, The Eighth Affiliated Hospital 
of Southern Medical University (The First People’s Hospital of Shunde Foshan), F, China 

Aims: Lecanemab, a monoclonal antibody targeting soluble amyloid-beta (Aβ) protofibrils, was introduced in China in 
June 2024. However, its real-world effectiveness and safety in the Chinese population remain to be fully elucidated, and 
optimal strategies for monitoring therapeutic response are yet to be established. This study aims to evaluate the 
effectiveness and safety of Lecanemab in clinical practice in China. 
Methods: This was a prospective, multicenter real-world study conducted across 23 centers. To better assess the 
treatment effect, a matched cohort from the Alzheimer' s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative was included for comparison. 
Participants received biweekly intravenous infusions of Lecanemab at a dose of 10 mg/kg. Comprehensive assessments 
were conducted, including neuropsychological evaluations, plasma biomarkers (Aβ42, Aβ40, P-Tau217, P-Tau181, else), 
and magnetic resonance imaging. For patients who provided consent, both Aβ and Tau-positron emission tomography 
scan imaging was performed after six months to evaluate pathological clearance. 
Results: As of August 2025, 261 participants who received at least one injection were enrolled (59.0% female; mean age 
69.74 ± 8.92 years; baseline MMSE 18.22 ± 6.1; 79.7% had CDR-GS at 0.5~1). Most plasma biomarkers exhibited 
significant treatment-related changes, with 82 participants completed assessments at 3 months, and 50 completed at 6 
months. Among 29 patients with PET-CT reassessment, mean summary Aβ decreased 42.9±6.2 centiloid and 41.4% 
converted to negative status. Notably, APOE ε4 non-carriers achieved greater clinical and biomarker improvements. The 
most frequent adverse event was infusion-related reactions (11.1%). Amyloid-related imaging abnormalities occurred in 
24 (9.2%) patients, with 4 (1.6%) being symptomatic, which did not differ significantly among participants with mild 
cognitive impairment (MCI) and moderate AD. 
Conclusions: Lecanemab was generally well-tolerated and the improvements in blood biomarkers suggest that it may 
have a beneficial impact on disease progression.

ANTI-AMYLOID THERAPY 

 

Alma Ghirelli1, Edoardo Gioele Spinelli2, Giordano Cecchetti1, Giulia Rugarli1, Stefano Pisano1, Federico Coraglia1, Ana 
Maria Samanes Gajate3, Andrea Panzacchi3, Gino Pepe4, Elisa Canu3, Veronica Castelnovo3, Elisa Sibilla3, Anna Gilioli3, 
Chiara Tripodi3, Fabiola Freri3, Paolo Vezzulli3, Sonia Calloni3, Andrea Falini3, Camilla Ferri3, Arturo Chiti4, Massimo 
Filippi5, Federica Agosta5 
1IRCSS San Raffaele Scientific Institute, Neurology, Milan, Italy, 2IRCCS San Raffaele Scientific Institute, Neurology, 
Milan, Italy, 3IRCCS San Raffaele Hospital, Milano, Italy, 4IRCCS San Raffaele Hospital, Nuclear Medicine, Milano, Italy, 
5Neurology Unit, Neurorehabilitation Unit, and Neurophysiology Service, Irccs Ospedale San Raffaele, Milan, Italy 

Aims: To assess baseline amyloid burden and regional SUVR patterns across AD phenotypes and their changes after 6 
months of anti-amyloid therapy. 
Methods: Twenty AD patients received lecanemab (n=8) or donanemab (n=12) for at least 6 months. Mean age was 69 
years; 60% female; mean disease duration 2.9 years. Fourteen patients had mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and six mild 
dementia. Clinical phenotypes included classic AD (n=10), early-onset AD (EOAD; n=8), primary progressive aphasia 
(PPA; n=1) and posterior cortical atrophy (PCA; n=1). Six patients (30%) were APOE ε4 heterozygous. Baseline MMSE 
was 24.8, CDR 0.6, CDR-SB 3. Baseline amyloid-PET centiloids averaged 87.1 (±23), with regional SUVRs extracted 
using Combinostics (reference: total cerebellum). ANCOVA models assessed SUVR differences across clinical 
phenotypes, adjusting for age and disease duration. Eleven patients completed 6-month follow-up PET scan. 
Results: Baseline centiloids did not differ between MCI (83.4) and mild dementia (95.6; p=0.29), including after 
adjustment. The highest baseline regional SUVRs were in anterior cingulate (1.68), followed by precuneus, prefrontal and 
parietal regions. After covariate adjustment, EOAD showed higher SUVRs than other phenotypes in prefrontal (p=0.01), 
lateral temporal (p=0.05), parietal (p=0.02), sensorimotor (p=0.02), and caudate (p=0.03) areas. At follow-up, six patients 
(all receiving donanemab; p=0.03) had PET negativity (<12 centiloids). Mean centiloid reduction was 64.7 for donanemab 
and 50.7 for lecanemab. MCI showed greater clearance than mild dementia (71.6 vs. 32.1; p=0.042), attenuated after 
adjustment (p=0.055). Regional clearance was higher in MCI than mild AD in prefrontal, parietal, occipital regions, and 
precuneus. No significant global or regional SUVR differences at 6 months were observed across phenotypes or 
treatment groups. 
Conclusions: Baseline and 6-month amyloid reduction varied by clinical phenotype. EOAD had higher baseline SUVRs. 
MCI had greater reductions than mild dementia.

title: IMMUNOTHERAPY FOR PARKINSON’S DISEASE AND ALZHEIMER’S DISEASE: A PROMISING DISEASE-
content:
VIRTUAL-184 

Topic: Theme B: Taupathies / B02.b. Therapeutic Targets, Mechanisms for Treatment: Immunotherapy 

IMMUNOTHERAPY FOR PARKINSON’S DISEASE AND ALZHEIMER’S DISEASE: A PROMISING DISEASE-
MODIFYING THERAPY 

 

Anns Mahboob1, Hasan Ali1, Aljazi Alnaimi1, Mahmoud Yousef2, Mlaak Rob3, Nawaf Al-Muhannadi1, Kalana 
Senevirathne1, Ali Chaari3 
1Weill-Cornell Medicine-Qatar, Doha, Qatar, 2Weill Cornell Medicine - Qatar, Doha, Qatar, 3Weill Cornell Medicine - Qatar, 
Medical, Doha, Qatar 

Aims: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and Parkinson’s disease (PD) are two of the most prevalent neurodegenerative 
disorders, contributing substantially to global morbidity, mortality, and socioeconomic burden. Current therapeutic 
strategies largely offer symptomatic relief without altering disease progression. This review aimed to evaluate the potential 
of antibody-based immunotherapies, particularly monoclonal antibodies (mAbs), as disease-modifying approaches for AD 
and PD, focusing on their mechanistic rationale, clinical progress, and future promise. 
Methods: A narrative review of recent preclinical and clinical studies was conducted, emphasizing immunotherapies that 
target pathological proteins implicated in AD and PD. Key targets included amyloid-beta (Aβ) and tau (τ) in AD, and alpha-
synuclein (α-syn) in PD. Data were synthesized to assess therapeutic efficacy, safety, and translational challenges, with 
particular attention to trial design, biomarker development, and patient stratification.  
Results: Emerging evidence suggests that mAbs targeting Aβ, tau, and α-syn hold promise in modifying disease 
trajectories. Clinical trials of Aβ-directed antibodies in AD have demonstrated reductions in amyloid burden and modest 
cognitive benefits, though safety concerns, particularly amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA), remain significant. 
For PD, α-syn–directed therapies are in earlier stages of development, with encouraging preclinical findings but limited 
clinical validation to date. Across both diseases, barriers to success include limited blood–brain barrier penetration, 
variable patient responses, and challenges in measuring disease-modifying outcomes.  
Conclusions: Monoclonal antibody–based immunotherapies represent a promising frontier for disease modification in AD 
and PD. While progress has been made, particularly in AD, substantial challenges remain before these therapies can be 
widely implemented. Future directions include combination approaches, refinement of biomarkers for early diagnosis and 
treatment monitoring, and the development of personalized therapeutic strategies to optimize efficacy and safety.

title: ALDH2 ACTIVATION ALLEVIATES NEUROINFLAMMATION AND NEURONAL APOPTOSIS

ALDH2 ACTIVATION ALLEVIATES NEUROINFLAMMATION AND NEURONAL APOPTOSIS 

POSTER ON BOARD - POSTER ON BOARD SHIFT 01: β-AMYLOID DISEASES / DISEASE 
MECHANISMS, PATHOPHYSIOLOGY / MICROGLIA 

Wu Kuan-Hsuan1, Ching-Chi Chiu1,2 
1Graduate Institute of Biomedical Science, College of Medicine, Chang Gung University, Taoyuan, 
Taiwan, 2Department of Medical Biotechnology and Laboratory Science, College of Medicine, Chang 
Gung University, Taoyuan, Taiwan 

Aims: Aldehyde dehydrogenase 2 (ALDH2) is a mitochondrial enzyme involved in removing reactive 
aldehydes generated during oxidative stress, such as 4-hydroxy-2-nonenal (4-HNE). ALDH2 also 
suppresses activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome pathway. ALDA-1, a small-molecule ALDH2 
activator, has demonstrated anti-inflammatory effects, potentially offering therapeutic benefits in 
neurodegenerative diseases. TOMM40, a mitochondrial outer membrane protein, has been 
associated with increased AD risk. In our previous study, we identified two TOMM40 missense 
mutations (F113L and F131L) from early-onset AD patients, both of which were found to impair 
mitochondrial function. In this study, we investigated the neuroprotective effects of ALDA-1 in BV2 
microglial cells expressing wild-type or mutant TOMM40. 

Methods: BV2 microglial cells were transfected with wild-type or mutant (F113L or F131L) TOMM40 
expression plasmids. BV2 microglia were pre-treated with ALDA-1 for 6 hours to assess its effects on 
mitochondrial function and inflammatory response. Mitochondrial ROS levels and mitochondrial 
membrane potential were measured using MitoSOX and TMRE molecular probes, respectively. Pro-
inflammatory cytokines were quantified using ELISA. To assess neurotoxicity, conditioned medium 
from treated or untreated BV2 cells was applied to HT22 hippocampal neurons, and cell viability was 
evaluated using the CCK-8 assay. 

Results: ALDA-1 restored ALDH2 activity and reduced 4-HNE accumulation in BV2 microglia 
expressing mutant TOMM40, thereby attenuating microglial activation and lowering the levels of pro-
inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, TNF-α, IL-6). In addition, ALDA-1 significantly reduced mitochondrial 
ROS production and restored mitochondrial membrane potential. Importantly, conditioned medium 
from ALDA-1-treated BV2 cells significantly alleviated the cell death of HT22 hippocampal neurons 
induced by conditioned medium from BV2 microglia expressing mutant TOMM40. 

Conclusions: These findings suggest that ALDH2 activation by ALDA-1 may serve as a potential 
therapeutic agent for preventing or treating AD by targeting microglial mitochondrial dysfunction and 
neuroinflammation.

Physikalische Biologie, Düsseldorf, Germany, 8Priavoid GmbH, Chief Medical Officer, Düsseldorf, 
Germany, 9Charite, 3department Of Psychiatry And Neuroscience, Memory Clinic, Berlin, Germany 

Aims: The drug candidate PRI-002 is an all-D-enantiomeric peptide and was developed to 
disassemble toxic Aβ oligomers into harmless Aβ monomers. It is anticipated that PRI-002 reduces 
neurotoxicity and restores synaptic plasticity in early stages of AD. In studies in healthy volunteers 
and in patients with early AD the orally administered PRI-002 has demonstrated to be safe and well 
tolerable. 

Methods: The PRImus-AD study (EU clinical trial number 2022-503148-41) is a randomized, double-
blind, placebo-controlled study to assess safety and efficacy of PRI-002 in patients with MCI or mild 
dementia due to Alzheimer’s Disease (AD). CSF or Amyloid-PET is used to confirm AD pathology. The 
trial is conducted in six European countries at 40 study sites. Eligible patients were randomly assigned 
(1:1:1) to receive 300 or 600 mg PRI-002 per day or placebo following an adaptive design for 48 to 96 
weeks of treatment duration. Stratification factors are disease state (MCI or mild dementia) and APOE 
e4 status. A follow-up assessment is planned 12 weeks after the end of treatment. In addition to the 
primary objective of safety, efficacy will be assessed based on the change from baseline to week 48 in 
global outcome as measured by CDR-SB. 

Results: 540 patients in total were screened. A screening failure rate of 42 % resulted in 304 eligible 
patients randomly assigned to the treatment arms. A blinded sample size recalculation confirmed the 
initial calculation of subjects to be enrolled. ARIA monitoring is closely performed for the first 90 
patients until week 24. 

Conclusions: Conclusion: The PRIMUS-AD phase 2 study enrolled 304 patients with MCI and mild 
dementia due to AD to assess safety and therapeutic benefit of PRI-002. Results are expected in Q3 
2026.

LECANEMAB FOR EARLY ALZHEIMER’S DISEASE: 48-MONTH RESULTS FOR APOE Ε4 NON-
CARRIERS OR HETEROZYGOTES FROM THE CLARITY AD OPEN-LABEL EXTENSION 

POSTER ON BOARD - POSTER ON BOARD SHIFT 01: β-AMYLOID DISEASES / DRUG 
DEVELOPMENT, CLINICAL TRIALS / AMYLOID CLEARANCE 

Lutz Froelich1, Shobha Dhadda2, Michio Kanekiyo2, Amanda Goodwin2, Mark Hodgkinson2, Steven 
Hersch2, Michael Irizarry2, Lynn Kramer2 
1Medical Faculty Mannheim, University of Heidelberg, Central Institute of Mental Health, Mannheim, 
Germany, 2Eisai Inc., Nutley, United States of America 

Aims: In Clarity AD, the Aβ-directed antibody lecanemab reduced markers of amyloid and slowed 
decline of cognition and function in early Alzheimer’s disease (AD). Lecanemab is associated with 
amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA), particularly in ApoE ε4 carriers. Herein, we report 48-
month findings from the ongoing Clarity AD open-label extension (OLE) study for ApoE ε4 non-carriers 
and heterozygotes. 

Methods: Clarity AD is an 18-month, randomized study (Core) followed by an OLE phase in individuals 
with early AD. Clinical (CDR-SB, ADAS-Cog14, and ADCS-MCI-ADL) outcomes and safety were 
evaluated from OLE data out to 48 months. Continued lecanemab treatment in the OLE was 
compared to matched control data from Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) data and 
the Swedish BioFINDER1 study. Results were evaluated in ApoE ε4 non-carriers and heterozygotes in 
Clarity AD. 

Results: In the ApoE ε4 non-carrier and heterozygote population, 1521 participants were treated with 
lecanemab across the Clarity AD Core and OLE. No new safety signals were observed. ARIA rates 
were low and after 6 months, were similar to ARIA rates on placebo. Lecanemab treatment continued 
to delay progression through 48 months compared to the matched control datasets, with differences 
in CDR-SB increasing over 18 months (ADNI:0.50; BioFINDER:0.66), 36 months (ADNI:0.87; 
BioFINDER:1.59), and 48 months (ADNI:1.53; BioFINDER:2.37). Consistent rates of clinical stability or 
improvements were observed across assessments regardless of baseline tau levels. Across the 48-
month period lecanemab reduced the relative risk of progression to next stage of disease versus 
matched placebo controls. 

Conclusions: In ApoE ε4 non-carriers and heterozygote treated with lecanemab through 48 months, 
there was an increasing treatment difference compared to matched control data, consistent with a 
disease-modifying effect. The long-term safety profile of lecanemab was confirmed.

(AD) AMONG PATIENTS INITIATING DONANEMAB IN THE REAL-WORLD

Ann Hartry1, Andrew Spargo1, Akash Bhushan2, Vamsi Chandra Kasivajjala3, Aparajeeta 
Priyadarasani4, Anand Srirampurapu2 
1Eli Lilly and Company, Indianapolis, United States of America, 2Neurodiscovery AI, Real-world 
Evidence & Research Analytics, Bangalore, India, 3Neurodiscovery AI, Alpharetta, United States of 
America, 4Neurodiscovery AI, London, United Kingdom 

Aims: Baseline characterization of patients initiating donanemab in the real world can provide 
insights into the application of appropriate use recommendations in routine care. This analysis 
summarizes pre-treatment MCI and AD diagnoses, MMSE scores, biomarker testing, and APOE 
genotype patterns. 

Methods: We performed a retrospective study of health record data (NeuroDiscovery) from patients 
receiving at least one dose of donanemab through Q3 2025. Pre-treatment diagnoses for MCI (G31.84) 
and AD (G30.x) were captured, and disease severity was classified using ICD-linked codes and MMSE 
categories. Age and gender were taken from the earliest pre-treatment record. Biomarker testing, 
including amyloid PET, CSF, and plasma measures, and APOE results were summarized. 

Results: The donanemab-treated cohort included 580 patients, with a balanced gender distribution 
(55.9% female) and a predominantly White population. Overall, 83.9% of patients were aged 71 years 
or older. MMSE data were available for 54% of patients, with scores consistent with MCI (MMSE>23) in 
49.5% of cases and with mild AD (MMSE 20-23) in 44.1%. Amyloid and P-tau biomarker results were 
available for nearly all patients. APOE genotyping was available for approximately half of the initiating 
patients, showing a higher proportion of non-ε4 carriers, followed by ε4 carriers and a smaller group of 
ε4 homozygous individuals. ICD-based classification at treatment initiation showed that 
approximately two-thirds of patients had an AD diagnosis, with the remaining one-third classified as 
MCI. The mean time from the most recent biomarker to treatment initiation was 52 days, and the 
mean time from the first biomarker to treatment was 225 days. 

Conclusions: This Real-world evidence study provides demographic and diagnostic distributions to 
support safety and effectiveness analyses as well as guidance for more efficient paths to appropriate 
treatment.

Aims: Olumiant® (baricitinib) was FDA/EMA-approved for rheumatoid arthritis, COVID, and alopecia 
areata. Assessment of this potent JAK inhibitor on biomarkers in AD could provide insights into the 
role of neuroinflammation in AD disease pathophysiology and progression. We tested both 
pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic biomarkers of baricitinib’s action in AD patients and 
compared them with a parallel arm of ALS patients as well as an asymptomatic carrier of a pathogenic 
C9ORF72 gene. 

Methods: NADALS was a prospective, observational, longitudinal, US study that enrolled adults with 
AD who initiated oral baricitinib. Participants were followed for 24 weeks to assess changes in 
established and candidate biomarkers, in relation to AD progression and baricitinib treatment. 
Assessments at screening, baseline and following 8 weeks (2 mg), and 16 and 24 weeks (4 mg), 
included biomarkers of AD pathology (Aβ, phospho-tau, and tau), inflammation, neuronal 
injury/death, smell function, cognitive function, and exploratory measures, including 32-marker 
phenotyping of immune cells in peripheral blood and CSF / serum proteomics with the SOMAlogic®, 
the Olink panel, and the NuLisa panel. Psychometric assessments were performed, and adverse 
events related to study procedures were tracked. 

Results: 13 AD patients were consented, of whom 7 AD patients provided ≥1 CSF sample. 6 
participants completed study procedures, 0 participants died, and 1 participant prematurely stopped 
participation. Biomarker and clinical data will be presented.

in baricitinib-treated patients with AD to inform an understanding of the association of brain exposure 
of baricitinib with peripheral and central inflammatory and neurodegenerative biomarkers in people 
with AD, ALS and asymptomatic gene carriers of C9ORF72.

Aims: Ensuring clinical trial populations represent the real-world diversity of people living with 
Alzheimer's disease (AD) is crucial to developing broadly beneficial therapies. This necessitates 
accessible trials that account for recruitment variations across demographics such as race, ethnicity, 
age, and sex. To achieve representative US enrolment in the Phase III trials of trontinemab in early 
symptomatic AD, TRONTIER 1 & TRONTIER 2, a data-driven approach for US site selection and 
recruitment planning was implemented. 

Methods: A SiteRx real-world database, encompassing healthcare provider, patient, site and 
recruitment funnel data from over 50 AD studies were analyzed. Sites were characterized using a 
composite measure of "enrolment potential" based on proximate volume of people with AD 
(community and site database) and historical enrolment. Proximate volume was overlaid on a map of 
the US to identify geographies with high volume and density of underrepresented AD populations. The 
planned site list was overlaid to inform site selection activities. Screening funnel modelling, based on 
13 previous AD trials with comparable inclusion/exclusion parameters, was performed to predict 
participant recruitment dynamics and calculate screen fail rates across protocol screening steps and 
demographic groups (race, ethnicity, age, and sex). 

Results: Site characterization identified approximately 150 AD trial sites with strong representative 
enrolment potential. Heat mapping data identified 15 US geographies where trial sites could be 
included to increase trial access to all demographic groups. Screening funnel modelling created a tool 
to predict the number of participants needed at each stage of screening to achieve representative 
enrolment, and identified conversion rate variations across demographic groups. 

Conclusions: Characterizing AD trial sites and modelling the screening funnel with real-world data 
provided valuable tools for data-driven US site landscaping and representative enrollment planning in 
the TRONTIER studies.

LONGITUDINAL TRENDS, AND THE EFFECTS OF DONEPEZIL 

POSTER ON BOARD - POSTER ON BOARD SHIFT 01: β-AMYLOID DISEASES / IMAGING, 
BIOMARKERS, DIAGNOSTICS / CSF, BLOOD, BODY FLUID BIOMARKERS 

William Baek 
Parkside Medical Group, Neurology, Upland, United States of America 

Aims: To investigate 1. Correlations between MMSE scores and p-tau181, p-tau217, and Abeta42/40 
ratio 2. Longitudinal trends in p-tau181, p-tau217, and Abeta42/40 ratio 3. If treatment affects p-
tau181, p-tau217, and Abeta42/40 ratio 

Methods: This was a retrospective chart review of 90 subjects diagnosed with AD between 2011 and 
2025. At least 2 MMSE scores and p-tau181 results were required. Both patients with pre- and post-
treatment BBM levels were included. 
Retrospective longitudinal correlation (Pearson, Spearman) analysis, per-subject linear slopes, 
mixed-effects models, paired pre→post changes (Wilcoxon) with p-values were used. 

Results: 29 subjects were included in the final analysis. Cross-sectional correlations were observed 
between MMSE and nearest BBM values; r ≈ −0.34 for p-tau181 and MMSE, r ≈ −0.31 for p-tau217 and 
MMSE, and r ≈ +0.40 for Abeta 42/40 and MMSE. Correlation within each subject was close to zero. 
Both p-tau181 and p-tau217 showed an increasing trend over time. Abeta42/40 ratio showed a 
decreasing trend. Among subjects with pretreatment baseline BBMs, Donepezil was associated with 
statistically significant reductions in p-tau181 and increases in Abeta42/40 ratio. p-tau217 did not 
show a significant change. 

Conclusions: Higher tau levels relate to worse and higher Abeta 42/40 ratio to better cognition. Both 
p-tau181 and p-tau217 showed an increasing trend over time, whereas Abeta42/40 ratio showed a 
decreasing trend, supporting the underlying pathology. No statistically significant correlations 
between MMSE and any BBM were observed at individual time points, though the direction of changes 
aligned with disease progression. Donepezil reduced p-tau181 levels and increased Abeta42/40 ratio, 
suggesting a change in the natural course of AD.

Research Unit, Department Of Clinical Sciences Malmö, Malmö, Sweden, 6F. Hoffmann-La Roche 
Ltd., Basel, Switzerland 

Aims: To investigate whether diffusion MRI (dMRI) can detect changes resulting from amyloid-
targeting immunotherapies. 

Methods: This study analyzed multimodal imaging data (PET, volumetric and dMRI) from a subset of 
participants of the phase 3 gantenerumab GRADUATE I and II trials. Despite not meeting primary 
clinical endpoints, graduate is a rich dataset to investigate imaging association. The relationship 
between free-water corrected dMRI metrics (mean diffusivity (MD(FWC)), fractional anisotropy (FA(FWC)), 
free-water fraction (FWF)), amyloid load, and brain volume were assessed in region-of-interest (ROI) 
(cortical gray, white matter, Mayo and Dickerson composite regions). Baseline associations were 
tested using Pearson's correlations. Longitudinally, individual slopes for dMRI metrics, global 
centiloids, and volume change (Jacobian integration) were calculated using linear mixed-effect 
models. Analyses included: 1) within-group “slope-slope” partial Pearson’s correlations to related 
dMRI changes to amyloid and volume changes, 2) region-wise Spearman’s correlations of net 
treatment effects (gantenerumab minus placebo) on amyloid removal and dMRI metrics, and 3) linear 
models on dMRI slopes to assess the main treatment effect (gantenerumab vs. placebo). All the 
metrics and the slopes were adjusted for age, sex, ApoE ε4 status, and Amyloid-Related Imaging 
Abnormalities (ARIA). 

Results: Participants in the gantenerumab-treated arm who exhibited faster global amyloid removal 
tended to show a decrease in FA(FWC) across most ROIs, along with increased rates of MD(FWC) in 
Mayo (Figure 1). Regions with greater net amyloid removal due to treatment demonstrated moderate 
greater relative net increases in MD(FWC) and FWF (Figure 2). The treatment analysis reported higher 
FWF rates in gantenerumab compared to placebo in white matter and Mayo (Figure 
3). 



 



 

 
Conclusions: This study shows novel longitudinal findings that dMRI metrics are dynamically altered 
by amyloid-targeting therapies.

Aims: To evaluate the effectiveness and safety of NeuralCIM® in patients with mild-to-moderate 
clinical Alzheimer's syndrome, amnesic variant, according to the 2011 National Institute on Aging - 
Alzheimer's Association (NIA-AA) criteria and under routine medical practice conditions. 

Methods: A multicenter, prospective, observational study was conducted under real-world 
conditions. NeuralCIM® was administered intranasally at 0.5 mg three times per week. 388 patients 
who reached week 52 of treatment and 187 patients who reached week 78 were evaluated. At 
baseline and at weeks 52 and 78, the following scales or instruments were performed: ADAScog11, 
CDR, GDS, MoCA, NPI, Cornell, Katz, Lawton, CIBIS (at baseline) and CIBIC plus (week 52 and 78). 

Results: At week 52, 66.0% of patients had improvement (≤ -4 points) and stability (≥ -3 and ≤1 point) 
according to ADAScog11. These results were maintained at week 78 with 63% of patients with 
improvement and stability. This contrasts with the natural evolution of the disease where without 
treatment almost 90% of patients worsen (≥2 points). Regarding the remaining instruments used 
(CDR, GDS, MoCA, NPI, Cornell, and CIBIC plus), 60% or more of patients showed improvement or 
maintained the same scores at both weeks 52 and 78. Katz and Lawton showed that more than 80% of 
patients maintained the same level of dependence with which they began this study in relation to 
basic and instrumental activities of daily living. This contrasts with the progression towards worsening 



 
in this neurodegenerative disease. The majority of adverse events were non-serious and mild intensity. 
Serious adverse events related to NeuralCIM® accounted for 4.7% of the total adverse events. 

Conclusions: NeuralCIM® shows encouraging results and a good safety profile in the treatment of 
mild-moderate clinical Alzheimer's syndrome, amnesic variant.

1Kobe City Medical Center General Hospital, Department Of Rehabilitation, Kobe, Japan, 2Kobe City 
Medical Center General Hospital, Department Of Neurology, Kobe, Japan, 3Kobe City Medical Center 
General Hospital, Department Of Psychiatry, Kobe, Japan 

Aims: To clarify domain-specific longitudinal changes in cognitive function in patients with early 
Alzheimer's disease (AD) treated with lecanemab, an anti–beta-amyloid monoclonal antibody, as 
these changes remain insufficiently characterized in real-world practice. 

Methods: We assessed early AD patients with confirmed amyloid pathology who received lecanemab 
at our institution between March 2024 and July 2025. Neuropsychological assessments included the 
Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE), Clinical Dementia Rating–Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB), Logical 
Memory (LM), Frontal Assessment Battery (FAB), Rey–Osterrieth Complex Figure (ROCF), Trail Making 
Test, and letter fluency. Scores at baseline (BL), 6 months (6M), and 12 months post-treatment were 
compared using a linear mixed-effects model with particular attention to changes from BL to 6M. 
Subscale scores were examined using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. 

Results: Twenty patients were included (mean age 75.8 years [SD 6.4]; 40% male; mean education 
13.1 years [SD 2.9]; mean CDR-SB 3.0 [SD 0.9]; APOE4: 50% heterozygotes, 15% non-carriers, 35% 
unknown). At 6 months post-treatment, MMSE declined (change −1.15, 95% CI −2.11 to −0.19, 
p=0.01), with a decrease in the Orientation subscale (p=0.02). CDR-SB also worsened (change +0.83, 
95% CI 0.27–1.39, p=0.002), mainly due to declines in the Orientation (p=0.02) and Judgement 
(p=0.01) subscales. Among memory measures, LM delayed recall declined (change −0.83, 95% CI 
−1.43 to −0.23, p=0.004). Only FAB improved (change +1.14, 95% CI 0.08–2.20, p=0.03), with an 
increase in the Luria Motor Series subtest (p=0.03). Other measures showed no significant change. 

Conclusions: In early AD patients treated with lecanemab, global cognition declined, particularly in 
orientation, and verbal memory also declined, whereas executive function showed potential 
improvement, most notably in motor programming.

University, Hun-ren Se Neuroepidemiological Research Group, Budapest, Hungary 

Aims: The aim of this retrospective cohort study was to provide a comprehensive overview of the 
current state of the healthcare system, placing emphasis on pharmacological treatment - especially 
memantine - utilisation patterns and their association with survival outcomes. 

Methods: Using the NEUROHUN database - containing inpatient, outpatient care data and pharmacy 
reports submitted for reimbursement - we conducted an analysis covering the entire population of 
Hungary between 2010 and 2020. Descriptive statistics, disease incidence and prevalence were 
calculated, followed by Kaplan-Meier analyses and Cox proportional hazard regression to evaluate 
survival outcomes. Sex, age at diagnosis, dementia subtypes, diagnosis switch, calculated adherence 
and persistence, and psychotropic drug use were also included as independent variables. All 
analyses were performed in R (version 4.5.1). 

Results: We identified 398,584 patients with a diagnosis of dementia between 2010 and 2020. The 
mean age at diagnosis was 75.22 years (SD = 12.110), and 63.7% of patients were female. Of the total 
cohort, only 13.3% (n=53,070) received anti-dementia medication (memantine, donepezil, or 
rivastigmine); 12,757 (24.0%) of these were on memantine monotherapy, the group with the highest 
rate of psychotropic prescriptions. Kaplan–Meier analysis showed the shortest median survival in 
untreated patients (3.105 years, 95% CI: 3.083 - 3.129), followed by those on memantine 
monotherapy among treated groups (3.704 years, 95% CI: 3.606 - 3.784). The multivariable Cox 
proportional hazards model revealed that patients receiving a combination of memantine and 
donepezil had the lowest mortality risk (HR: 0.581, 95% CI: 0.566-0.597) compared to the untreated 
group. 

Conclusions: These findings suggest a high proportion of delayed diagnoses, as memantine is 
indicated in advanced dementia stages. Timely diagnosis—particularly in the era of emerging disease-
modifying therapies—along with evidence-based healthcare planning is therefore inevitable.

DISCOVERY OF IGS01, A HIGHLY SELECTIVE MUSCARINIC ACETYLCHOLINE M4 RECEPTOR 
POSITIVE ALLOSTERIC MODULATOR (PAM) WITH A FAVORABLE DDI RISK PROFILE FOR 
PSYCHOSIS 

POSTER ON BOARD - POSTER ON BOARD SHIFT 01: PSYCHIATRIC SYMPTOMS IN 
NEURODEGENERATIVE DISEASES / DRUG DEVELOPMENT, CLINICAL TRIALS 

Junliang Hao, Yishan Sun, Chao Wang, Ye Tian, Jiayin Li, Qiong Tan, Pengcheng Huang, Q. Kevin Fang 
Ignis Therapeutics, Shanghai, China 

Aims: Differentiated from standard-of-care antipsychotics, muscarinic acetylcholine M4 receptor 
modulators have sparked significant interest for their potential to provide a superior benefit-risk 
profile in treating psychosis. Positive and selective modulation of the M4 receptor fine-tunes neural 
circuits underlying psychosis while minimizing gastrointestinal and other side effects associated with 
stimulation of other muscarinic subtypes. The selective M4 PAM emraclidine demonstrated efficacy 
signals in Phase 1b, but missed endpoints in two Phase 2 studies, triggering multifaceted re-thinking 
on better ways to harness the M4-PAM MoA. One noteworthy aspect of emraclidine is its exclusive 
metabolism by CYP3A4, which raises concerns about potential drug-drug interactions (DDIs) and 
limits its use in geriatric patients (e.g. AD psychosis). To overcome this limitation, Ignis initiated a 
program to identify a selective M4 PAM with reduced DDI liability. 

Methods: A SAR campaign guided by an internally resolved cryo-EM structure of the emraclidine-M4-
Gi complex was conducted. Compounds were advanced through a flow scheme that focused on 
ADME properties and DDI risk assessment. 

Results: IGS01 displayed comparable potency to emraclidine in a human M4 cAMP assay with 
minimal activities at other muscarinic receptors and across a 98-target secondary pharmacology 
panel. In preclinical studies, IGS01 dose-dependently reversed amphetamine induced 
hyperlocomotion and rescued amphetamine induced sensory gating deficits in rats. It exhibited 
favorable PK properties with low to moderate in vivo clearance (m/r/d/mky). Importantly, IGS01 was 
metabolized by multiple CYP isoforms with a fm,cyp3A4 < 0.5, suggesting significantly lower DDI risk 
compared to emraclidine. 

Conclusions: IGS01 has completed GLP toxicology studies en route to an IND application. It 
represents a new opportunity to harness M4 activation for the treatment of psychosis in geriatric 
patients that demands a favorable DDI risk profile.

Aims: Bepranemab is a recombinant, humanised, full-length immunoglobulin G4 monoclonal 
antibody, targeting a mid-region tau epitope essential for tau aggregation. We describe results from 
two open-label extension (OLE) studies assessing long-term safety of bepranemab in Alzheimer’s 
disease (TOGETHER OLE [NCT04867616]) and in progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), a rapidly 
progressing neurodegenerative disorder (PSP002 [NCT04658199]). 

Methods: TOGETHER was a, global, multicentre, placebo-controlled, Phase II study. Following the 80-
week double-blind period, participants entering the 48-week OLE continued the same bepranemab 
dose, or if previously on placebo, were re-randomised 1:1 to bepranemab 45/90 mg/kg (intravenous 
[IV] every 4 weeks [Q4W]) for ≤44 weeks, followed by a safety follow-up period (20 weeks after the last 
infusion). The OLE focused on long-term safety, including treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) 
from OLE Baseline to study end. PSP002 was an OLE of PSP003 (NCT04185415), a double-blind, 
placebo-controlled, Phase Ib study of bepranemab (90 mg/kg, IV Q4W over 48 weeks) in PSP. In 
PSP002, participants (aged ≥40 years) met Movement Disorder Society-PSP criteria for 
possible/probable PSP and completed the PSP003 treatment period. Exclusion criteria included 
meeting mandatory withdrawal and/or stopping criterion in PSP003. PSP002 primary endpoint: 
incidence of TEAEs from OLE Baseline to Month 60. 

Results: TOGETHER: Of the 466 participants randomised into TOGETHER, 387 participants were 
dosed during the OLE period and 312 completed the OLE period. PSP002: Of the 25 participants 
randomised into PSP003, 19 entered the OLE; the PSP002 study is ongoing with a small number of 
participants. Safety results from the TOGETHER and PSP002 OLEs will be presented. 



 
Conclusions: Results from the TOGETHER and PSP002 OLEs will provide further information about 
the long-term safety of bepranemab.

on Tau pathology and cognitive decline (discussed by Höglinger, abstract #776 ). This abstract 
summarizes key findings from these developments and presents the rationale and design of NIDB-

Aims: Transmembrane protein 106B (TMEM106B) is a lysosomal membrane protein expressed in 
neurons and glia. Recent studies have shown that the C-terminal domain of TMEM106B forms 
amyloid filaments in the brain of patients with various neurodegenerative diseases (NDDs), including 
tauopathies, β-amyloid-, α-synuclein-, and TDP-43-proteinopathies, as well as in elderly individuals 
without brain disease, in an age dependent manner. Whether the filaments contribute to 
pathogenesis or are only bystanders in disease, remains unclear. Genetic variants in TMEM106B are 
linked to an altered risk for frontotemporal dementia and Alzheimer’s disease. A threonine-to-serine 
substitution at position 185 (TMEM106B T185S; rs3173615 C>G) has been associated with a 
protective effect. The cellular mechanisms underlying the risk-modulating effect are still elusive. 

Methods: Here, cellular mechanisms of the TMEM106B rs3173615 variant will be investigated in 
human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) -derived microglia (iMG), brain biopsies of idiopathic 
normal pressure hydrocephalus (iNPH) patients, and postmortem brain samples of NDD patients. 
iPSCs were generated from skin fibroblasts of individuals who are homozygous carriers of the 
protective allele (GG) and non-carriers (CC). The iPSCs will be differentiated into iMG and treated with 
lipopolysaccharide (LPS), followed by omics-analyses and functional experiments. Cortical biopsies 
from iNPH patients and postmortem brain samples from NDD patients carrying rs3173615 CC, CG, or 
GG, will be examined using immunohistochemical stainings including IBA1, β-amyloid, CD68, LAMP1, 
GFAP, synapsin I, TDP-43, and TMEM106B antibodies. 

Results: Staining of inferior temporal cortex samples of 78 NDD patients with TMEM106B C-terminal 
antibody revealed that TMEM106B accumulation was significantly increased in later Braak stages V-VI 
compared to stages I-IV. 

Conclusions: Forthcoming analyses aim to clarify how the rs3173615 variant influences TMEM106B 
function, filament formation, and its role in neurodegeneration.

Aims: Valiltramiprosate/ALZ-801, a valine-conjugated prodrug of tramiprosate that prevents Aβ toxic 
oligomer formation, was evaluated in APOE4/4 homozygotes with Early AD. APOE4 is a risk factor for 
cerebral amlyloid angiopathy and ARIA. This 78-week placebo-controlled trial included subjects with 
any number of baseline microhemorrhages (MH) and several superificial siderosis lesions. 

Methods: APOE4/4 homozygotes with Early AD (MMSE ≥22) were randomized 1:1 (placebo:265 mg 
BID), MRIs were conducted every 26 weeks, with centralized evaluations for ARIA-E/H. Anti-platelets 
were allowed, anti-coagulants were exclusionary. 

Results: Safety population (N=325); 51% females, 89% Caucasian, mean age 68 years, MMSE 25.6; 
298 had screening/baseline and 290 had post-treatment MRI. At baseline, 32% had >1 MH (placebo, 
32%, active, 31%); 11% of placebo and 8% active had siderosis (maximum 4 and 5 lesions, 
respectively); and 5% per/arm had ≥ 10 MH. ARIA-E occurred in 5 subjects/arm (3%) and 
macrohemorrhages in 2 subjects/arm. Increase in MH from low to high category (0, 1-4, 5-9, ≥10 MH) 
occurred in 14% placebo and 9% active. Radiographically all ARIA-E were mild except 1 severe 
(placebo) and 1 moderate (active), and all ARIA-E/H events were asymptomiatic. AEs with incidence 
>5% and >2x placebo rate were nausea (26%), weight decrease (14%), decreased appetite and 
vomiting (10% each); with lower headache, falls and dizziness rates in active arm. 

Conclusions: Valiltramiprosate was well tolerated with favorable safety over 78 weeks consistent 
with prior studies in >3000 AD patients. ARIA-E rates were similar between valiltramiprosate and 
placebo arms (~3%), ARIA-H was lower than placebo, and no ARIA events were symptomatic. 
Coupled with promising efficacy in MCI subjects, valiltramiprosate provides a favorable benefit-risk 
profile for high-risk APOE4/4 patients with unmet need for safe and effective disease-modifying 
treatments.

Aims: Valiltramiprosate/ALZ-801, an oral anti-amyloid oligomer agent was evaluated in 78-week 
Phase 3 trial in APOE4/4 homozygotes with Early AD. In overall population valiltramiprosate did not 
show clinical efficacy but showed significant slowing of brain atrophy on volumetric MRI. Pre-
specified MCI subgroup showed positive clinical and vMRI effects. Brain microstructural integrity was 
evaluated using diffusion tensor imaging (MRI-DTI). 

Methods: Study enrolled 325 homozygotes (162 placebo, 163 valiltramiprosate); ~40% were MCI 
(MMSE >26) and 60% Mild AD (MMSE, 22-26). ADAS-Cog13 and CDR-SB were primary and key 
secondary outcomes, respectively; hippocampal volume (HV) was the main vMRI outcome. Mean 
water diffusivity (DTI-MD) in grey and white matter (GM,WM) were centrally analyzed by Clario Inc. 
Lower DTI-MD indicates tissue preservation. MMRM was primary analysis; Pearson’s correlations were 
conducted. 

Results: Clinical/vMRI datasets included 320/290 subjects respectively; DTI included 85 MCI, 123 
Mild subjects. In overall population, valiltramiprosate effects on MD showed positive trends in 4 GM 
regions (p<0.1), and significant WM effects [corpus callosum genu (GCC) (p<0.001), fornix (p=0.007), 
corpus callosum (p=0.023), and corona radiata (p=0.037)]. MCI showed GM effects in caudate 
(p=0.0095) and cingulate cortex (p=0.015); WM effects in GCC/whole CC/splenium CC 
(p=0.003/0.014/0.037), fornix (p=0.032), and corona radiata (p=0.042). In MCI active arm, MD effects 
in several GM/WM areas correlated significantly with clinical (correlations ≥0.34, p<0.03) and 
volumetric measures (≥ 0.56, p<0.001).

grey/white matter regions, most prominent in areas affected early in MCI (cingulate cortex/ 
fornix/corpus callosum). These effects correlated significantly with its positive clinical/brain-volume 
benefits, suggesting preservation of the brain’s microstructural integrity. Together, these imaging 



 
findings suggest slowing of neurodegeneration, and support valiltramiprosate’s efficacy in APOE4/4 
MCI patients.

Aims: Valiltramiprosate, an oral small molecule inhibitor of amyloid-beta (Aβ) oligomer formation, 
was evaluated in a 78-week trial in APOE4/4 homozygotes with Early AD. Since hippocampus atrophy 
occurs early in APOE4/4 homozygotes, hippocampal volume (HV) was the main imging outcome. 
Correlations of valiltramiprosate effects on vMRI with its effects on clinical outcomes are presented 
over 78 weeks. 

Methods: This double-blind trial randomized 325 subjects 1:1 (valiltramiprosate 265 mg BID/ 
placebo); stratified by MCI (MMSE 27-30) or Mild AD (MMSE 22-26). ADAS-Cog13 was the primary with 
key secondary/secondary functional outcomes (CDR-SB, DAD). Volumetric MRI measures, including 
HV, cortical thickness/whole brain volumes (CT, WBV) were collected every 26 week and centrally 
analyzed. MMRM was main analysis model; analysis by disease stages was pre-specified. Spearman’s 
correlations are presented. 

Results: In overall population, primary and secondary clinical outcomes were not significant but all 
vMRI outcomes showed significant atrophy slowing versus placebo (HV, 18% less atrophy, p=0.017). 
Prespecified, MCI (MMSE 27-30, N=125), showed positive effects/trends on ADAS-Cog13 (52%, 
p=0.041), DAD (96%, p=0.016) and CDR-SB (102%, p=0.053); with significant atrophy slowing in HV 
(26%), CT (35%), both p< 0.01, and in WBV (22%, p=0.027). In active arm, subject-level correlations 
between HV-ADAS (r=-0.40), HV-CDR (r=-0.45) were both significant (p<0.005); clinical correalations 
for CT, WBV were also significant (coefficients 0.34-0.49). 

Conclusions: In APOLLOE4 pre-specified MCI group, valiltramiprosate showed nominally significant 
cognitive and functional benefits with significant atrophy slowing in all brain compartments (HV 26%, 
WBV 22%). Hippocampal and whole-brain volume effects showed significant subject-level 



 
correlations with cognitive and functional benefits over 78 weeks (correlations 0.45-0.49). In the MCI 
population with adequate neuronal reserve, valiltramiprosate effects on neurodegeneration translate 
to meaningful clinical efficacy with favorable safety in APOE4/4 homozygotes.

Aims: Background: Autolysosomal dysfunction is increasingly recognized as a key mechanism for 
neurodegenerative disorders such as AD and PD pathogenesis. TML-6, a synthetic curcumin analog, 
targets this mechanism by restoring lysosomal acidification and promoting β-amyloid and α-synuclein 
clearance. Objective: To evaluate the therapeutic effects of TML-6 in AD/PD animal models and in the 
Phase 2 trial design of AD and PD. 

Methods: The lysosomal integrity was damaged by the lysosomotropic reagent l-leucyl-l-leucine 
methyl ester (LLOMe) or bafilomycin A1, and Aβ and α-synuclein was used to evaluate the phagocytic 
lysosomal responses in primary neural cell and microglia cultures. The effect of TML-6 on a PD animal 
model was conducted. The Phase 2 AD trial is conducted and will recruit 210 subjects with MCI or 
mild dementia of AD. Participants will be treated with oral TML-6. Endpoints include 
neuropsychological assessments and blood biomarkers. The phase 2 results of TML-6 in AD will be 
extended to PD treatment in 2028. 

Results: TML-6 demonstrated the ability to rescue lysosomal function and facilitate both intracellular, 
extracellular Aβ and α-synuclein clearance in neurons and microglia. The effect of TML-6 on PD 
animal model revealed promising behavior improvement and α-synuclein reduction. Following Phase 
1 data showing favorable safety and pharmacokinetics in elderly subjects, a global Phase 2 trial for AD 
(U.S., Sweden, Taiwan) will be conducted after FDA approval. The trial success of phase 2 in AD will 
then be extended to phase 2 trial in 2028 for PD. 

Conclusions: TML-6 exhibits a multi-target action mechanism by driving autolysosomal regulation to 
remove the mutant protein accumulation in neuron and microglia, meeting the new era strategy to be 
developed as potential breakthrough drugs for neurodegenerative diseases in AD and PD therapy.

Aims: LEAD is an investigator- led,multicenter, prospective, real-world study to avaluate effectiveness 
and safety of Lecanemab. The primary objective was to assess the effectiveness of lecanemab under 
real-world clinical practice in early Alzheimer's diseasepatients in China. The secondary objectives 
included evaluating the safety of lecanemab for the management of AD in Chinese patients in terms 
of adverse events (AEs), serious AEs along with discontinuation of lecanemab. 

Methods: This multicentre, prospective cohort trial included participants 40 to 90 years old with early 
AD (MCI or mild dementia due to AD) having an indication for lecanemab. Each participant had 
evidence of PET or by CSF. Baseline data on demographics, medical history, quality of life, cognitive 
score, plasma biomarkers, Apoe and neuroimaging indicators were assessed and a treatment with 
intravenous lecanemab (10 mg per kilogram of body weight each 2 weeks) was started. The patients 
will be followed up after three, six and twelve months including safety visits, provide blood samples to 
measure AD biomarkers at months. All cognitive assessments will be repeated at month 6 and 12. The 
last study visit will be at week 52, when all baseline measurements will be repeated. 

Results: From August 2024 to present, the research is still ongoing, After 6 months of treatment, 
MMSE (0.821, p=0.013) and ADL (-4.605, p<0.001) showed significant improvement compared to the 
baseline, the plasma pTau 217/Aβ 42 and pTau 181/Aβ 42 ratios were significantly reduced (p<0.001) 
and the plasma Aβ 42 concentration was significantly increased (p<0.001). Adverse reactions 
occurred in 22 cases (ARIA-H 7%, ARIA-E 2%, infusion-related reactions (fever 3%, allergy 1%)). 

Conclusions: The existing results suggest that Lecanemab treatment for early Alzheimer's disease 
(AD) shows clinical symptom and plasma biomarkers improvement at 6 month.

Aims: Progressive hippocampal atrophy is a hallmark of Alzheimer’s disease (AD). 
Valiltramiprosate/ALZ-801 is an oral, small-molecule inhibitor of amyloid-oligomer formation in 
development as a disease-modifying treatment for early symptomatic AD. While the APOLLOE4 Phase 
3 trial did not meet the primary cognitive endpoint in the overall Early AD population, valiltramiprosate 
showed significant slowing of atrophy in hippocampus and all other brain regions. Also, the 
prespecified Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) subgroup (MMSE >26) showed meaningful, (nominally) 
significant clinical benefits that correlated with significant reduction in hippocampal atrophy. 
Responder analysis was conducted on a subgroup of super-responders who showed increased 
hippocampal volume (HV) over baseline at 78 weeks. 

Methods: APOLLOE4 was a randomized, double-blind, 78-week, placebo-controlled Phase 3 trial 
conducted in 325 APOE4/4 homozygotes (MMSE 22-30). Valiltramiprosate 265 mg or placebo was 
administered BID. Primary outcome was ADAS-Cog13, and HV by vMRI was the main imaging 
outcome. Super-responders were defined as an increase in HV at 78 weeks over baseline. 

Results: Early symptomatic completers with ≥26 MMSE included 10/64 and 2/67 subjects in active 
and placebo arms, respectively. This represents 16% active and 3% placebo super-responders. One 
active super-responder had an MMSE of 24. The valiltramiprosate super-responders (6M/5F) showed a 
larger HV (Δ +66.0±20.4 mm3) at 78 weeks and exhibited younger age, higher baseline MMSE, and 
larger baseline HV than overall early symptomatic population. The HV-rescuing benefit was 
associated with improved ADAS-Cog13 and CDR-SB. 

Conclusions: Valiltramiprosate reversed hippocampal atrophy and stabilized cognition/function over 
78 weeks in a subgroup of early symptomatic AD subjects. The increased HV in this subgroup 
suggests a beneficial effect of valiltramiprosate on neurogenesis/neuroplasticity and supports its 
potential as a preventive treatment for APOE4/4 presymptomatic AD patients.

Cloud (OM1, Inc., Boston, MA), a real-world dataset with linked claims and electronic medical record 
(EMR) data on patients in the US. The study population included adult patients initiating donanemab 
between July 2024 and September 2025, the first 15 months following FDA approval. Patients were 
also required to have a recorded diagnosis of mild cognitive impairment or Alzheimer's disease and at 
least one claim or EMR encounter in the 365 days prior to treatment initiation. Baseline 
characteristics of donanemab initiators were tabulated and included demographics, insurance type, 
clinical comorbidities, medication use and use of diagnostic testing procedures. 

Results: The final eligible cohort comprised 1,143 patients [mean age in years (standard deviation 
(SD)) = 76.6 (6.4)] who initiated donanemab. Patients were predominantly female (53.4%), white race 
(93.7%), and resided in the South (74.8%). 63.9% had a diagnosis of MCI and 81.5% had a diagnosis of 
AD, reflecting real-world coding patterns and the inability to capture exact disease severity. The first 
dose for most patients (71.6%) was 350 mg, consistent with the modified dosing regimen. 
Comorbidities were frequent with most common being dyslipidemia (78.9%), hypertension (71.3%) 
and prior malignancy (27.7%). 

Conclusions: This cohort study provides insights into the early initiators of donanemab in routine 
care. Since the characteristics of the study population reflect the specific data source used, findings 
may not be broadly generalizable. Additional analyses of donanemab utilization and monitoring during 
follow-up will be presented at the conference.

Shinshu University School of Medicine, Neurology & Rheumatology, Matsumoto city, Japan 

Aims: To investigate the effect of anti-Aβ therapy by quantifying annual brain volume changes using 
Synthetic MRI (SyMRI). 

Methods: Patients diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and treated with Lecanemab or 
Donanemab were enrolled. SyMRI was performed at baseline and subsequently at 1, 2, 3, 6, and 12 
months post-treatment initiation. Quantitative analysis using SyMRI NEURO® included measurements 
of brain parenchymal volume (BPV), intracranial volume (ICV), brain parenchymal fraction (BPF; 
calculated as BPV/ICV), gray matter volume fraction (GM), white matter volume fraction (WM), and 
myelin volume fraction (MY). Longitudinal changes were analyzed using a generalized linear mixed 
model, with time since treatment initiation as the fixed effect. 

Results: A total of 24 patients were enrolled; 13 completed the 6-month follow-up, and 6 completed 
the 12-month evaluation. At baseline, the mean (range) age, Mini-Mental State Examination-Japanese 
(MMSE-J) score, and BPF were 69.5 years (53–87), 24.6 (21–29), and 75.8% (69.9–82.9), respectively. 
There was a moderate association between BPF and MMSE-J (r = 0.463, 95% confidence interval: 
0.113–0.783). The mean coefficient of variation (CV) for ICV across time points was 0.67%. Annualized 
changes in MMSE-J, BPF, GM, WM, and MY were 0.7 ± 0.7, -1.4% ± 0.2%, 1.5% ± 0.6%, -2.0% ± 1.0%, 
and -0.3% ± 0.4% (mean ± standard error), respectively. Three participants experienced ARIA-H within 
one year, all cases being mild without significant differences in baseline parameters compared to 
those without ARIA. 

Conclusions: SyMRI-based measurements showed low CV, indicating strong test-retest reliability. 
The annual decline in BPF matched rates previously reported for mild cognitive impairment patients 
and GM remained more stable than WM.

Aims: To assess plasma GFAP levels as a biomarker for anti-inflammatory effects and cognitive 
improvement following treatment with troculeucel, an autologous, non-genetically modified NK cell 
therapy with enhanced cytotoxicity and activating receptor expression, in Alzheimer’s disease (AD) 
patients enrolled in Phase 1 studies. 

Methods: In a Phase 1 dose-escalation study (NCT04678453; n=10), troculeucel was administered 
intravenously every three weeks for 3 months (4 doses at 1B, 2B, or 4B). In a separate Phase 1 study 
(NCT06189963; n=3), moderate AD patients received 6B cells every three weeks for 12 months. 
Plasma GFAP levels, an inflammatory marker in neurodegenerative disease, along with cognitive 
scores (ADCOMS and CDR-SB) were collected at baseline and 3 months post-treatment. Correlation 
analyses were performed to evaluate relationships between GFAP levels and cognitive performance. 

Results: At baseline, plasma GFAP levels showed strong, statistically significant positive correlations 
with cognitive scores: CDR-SB (r=0.60, p=0.045) and ADCOMS (r=0.64, p=0.030). After 3 months of 
troculeucel treatment, correlations remained strong: CDR-SB (r=0.57, p=0.056) and ADCOMS (r=0.66, 
p=0.022). The consistency in correlation strength and direction across both timepoints indicates that 
plasma GFAP levels are closely associated with cognitive status in AD patients. 

Conclusions: These findings suggest plasma GFAP is a responsive biomarker for monitoring the anti-
inflammatory effects of troculeucel and its cognitive benefits in AD. The data support troculeucel’s 
therapeutic potential and highlight plasma GFAP as a valuable indicator of treatment efficacy in early-
phase clinical trials.

DIAGNOSTICS:  CSF- AND BLOOD-BASED BIOMARKERS 

Hugo Vanderstichele, June Kaplow, Maddelyn Hyland, James Doherty, Jasna Jerecic 
Acumen Pharmaceuticals, Newton, United States of America 

Aims: Biofluid biomarkers are used to evaluate efficacy and mechanism of action of disease-
modifying drugs and are transformative in the diagnosis of Alzheimer’s disease (AD). We conducted 
an evaluation of biomarker changes after treatment with the AβO-selective antibody sabirnetug 
(ACU193) in the phase 1 randomized, placebo-controlled INTERCEPT-AD study in early symptomatic 
AD using the NULISAseq™ CNS Disease Panel v1 to confirm and expand our understanding of changes 
in neuronal protein levels. 

Methods: Biomarkers were measured in CSF and EDTA-plasma pre- and post-dose. Percent change in 
NPQ units from baseline to endpoint for the 127 analytes was compared between treatment groups 
and placebo using two-sample Welch’s t-tests. No adjustments were made for multiplicity therefore 
statistical significance is considered nominal. Spearman’s rank correlation analyses assessed 
relationships amongst and between protein proteoforms (Aß, tau, phosphorylated tau, neurofilament) 
over time across all dose groups as well as the correlation of ELISA and NULISA results. 

Results: Published biomarker results from INTERCEPT-AD were confirmed and extended with 
NULISA. A treatment effect was shown for pTau217 in CSF. In EDTA-plasma, treatment effects were 
observed for GFAP, Aß38, Aß40, Aß42, and for the ratio of tau/Aß42, pTau181/Aß42, and pTau217/Aß42. 
Positive correlations were obtained in CSF between and amongst the different Aß (Aß38, Aß40, Aß42), 
tau (total Tau, pTau181, pTau217, pTau231), and neurofilament (NF-L, NF-H) proteoforms. A negative 
correlation was seen between Aß42/Aß40 and pTau181. Previously reported results correlated with 
NPQ values measured with NULISA. 

Conclusions: AT(N) biomarker correlations were identified between different proteoforms of Aß and 
pTau. Aß38, pTau231 and NFL-H/L, amongst other candidate proteins, were identified as novel 
pharmacodynamic biomarkers. The results further support the downstream pathophysiological 
changes affected by sabirnetug treatment in AD.

title: LONGITUDINAL EFFECTS OF ALZHEIMER’S DISEASE MEDICATION ON COGNITIVE OUTCOMES
content:

LONGITUDINAL EFFECTS OF ALZHEIMER’S DISEASE MEDICATION ON COGNITIVE OUTCOMES 

POSTER ON BOARD - SHIFT 02: β-AMYLOID DISEASES / THERAPEUTIC TARGETS, MECHANISMS 
FOR TREATMENT / ABETA, TRUNCATED & PGLU-ABETA 

Jenny Jyoung Lee1, Anisha Das2, Yuanjia Wang3, Annie Lee2 
1Ewha Womans University, Department Of Data Science, Seoul, Korea, Republic of, 2Columbia 
University, Department Of Neurology, New York, United States of America, 3Columbia University, 
Department Of Biostatistics, New York, United States of America 

Aims: The long-term effectiveness of Alzheimer’s disease (AD) medications on cognition and brain 
health remains uncertain, particularly when accounting for the dynamic nature of treatment 
exposure. To address this gap, we leveraged longitudinal data from the Harvard Aging Brain Study–
Healthy Diversity (HABS-HD) cohort to examine the effect of longitudinal AD medication exposure on 
changes in cognition, dementia severity, and white matter hyperintensity (WMH) volume using data-
driven approach. 

Methods: Eligible HABS-HD participants with mild cognitive impairment were analyzed. Cognitive 
outcomes included CDR Sum of Boxes (CDR-Sum), MMSE, Digit Symbol Substitution Test (DDST), and 
WMH volume. Longitudinal trajectories were modeled with linear mixed-effects model among AD 
medication initiators or discontinuers (n=148). As treatment decisions are influenced by worsening 
cognition, MSMs were applied to address time-varying confounding and to achieve baseline covariate 
balance, enabling causal effect estimation of continued treatment versus no treatment in a larger 
sample (n=367). 

Results: AD medication users exhibited slower cognitive decline and disease progression, with less 
worsening of CDR-Sum (β=–3.83), higher MMSE (β=5.96), improved DSST (β=1.39), and attenuated 
WMH progression (β=–1.55). In the larger cohort, MSMs confirmed consistent effects, including lower 
CDR-Sum (α=–4.26), higher MMSE (α=5.28), and improved DSST (α=1.12). Overall, continued AD 
medication use was associated with broadly protective cognitive and neuroimaging profiles, 
underscoring its potential to mitigate decline and modify disease progression. 

Conclusions: Our study demonstrates that initiation or discontinuation of AD medications was 
associated with slower short-term cognitive decline, and continued use had a causal effect on 
sustaining cognitive function and slowing neuroimaging progression over the longer term. These 
results highlight the clinical value of both early intervention and continued adherence, and also 
illustrates how causal modeling approaches can enhance the evaluation of AD therapies.

Italy, 4Department of Pathology and Molecular Medicine, Queen's University, Kingston,

United States of America 

Aims: To test whether a novel machine learning method can surface patient subpopulations with 
differential response within a negative Alzheimer’s disease trial and to deconstruct those populations 
into explainable and unexplainable subgroups. 

Methods: A sub-insight learning approach was applied to the Anti-Amyloid Treatment in 
Asymptomatic Alzheimer’s Disease (A4) dataset to identify subpopulations defined by 2–4 variables 
predictive of treatment response. A4 enrolled clinically asymptomatic older adults with amyloid 
pathology randomized to solanezumab or placebo, with the primary outcome being change in the 
Preclinical Alzheimer Cognitive Composite (PACC) Total Score through Week 240. A subsample 
comprising participants with cognitive impairment at follow-up (n=51) and without (n=100) was 
analyzed. 

Results: Two subpopulations demonstrated less decline with solanezumab at Week 240. Subgroup 1 
(n=20, 26% of the testing sample) was defined by higher right amygdala volume and higher baseline 
PACC Digit Symbol Substitution Test scores (Cohen’s d=1.1, p=.03). Subgroup 2 (n=9, 12% of the 
testing sample) was defined by higher right superior temporal lobe volume and higher baseline PACC 
Digit Symbol Substitution Test scores (Cohen’s d=2.3, p=.03). These findings suggest that individuals 
with higher brain volume and higher cognitive function at baseline may benefit most from 
solanezumab. 

Conclusions: An explainable ML strategy identified clinically interpretable profiles that may be 
preferential responders to solanezumab, despite the overall negative A4 result. These exploratory 
findings, based on limited sample sizes, suggest that greater regional brain volume and stronger 
psychomotor speed/attention at baseline may enrich for treatment benefit. Independent replication, 
presentation of absolute subgroup counts, and adjustment for multiplicity are warranted; if 
confirmed, this approach could support precision enrichment in future preclinical AD trials.

Aims: ARIA may occur in patients treated with anti-amyloid therapies. This study reports ARIA 
incidence and patient characteristics among Veterans treated with lecanemab (LEC) in the VAHS. 

Methods: Veterans receiving LEC infusions through July 2025 in VAHS and community care, but not 
Medicare-covered beneficiaries, were included. ARIA was ascertained by radiologists. Clinical notes 
were reviewed under neurologist/neuroradiologist guidance to report ARIA incidence and attributes. 
Structured data were assessed to describe patient characteristics. 

Results: 117 Veterans receiving LEC was identified with mean age 73.7 years, 96.6% male, 90.6% 
white, and 90.6% non-Hispanic. Top baseline comorbidities included hypertension (64.1%), 
hypercholesterolemia (47.9%), diabetes (28.2%), cerebrovascular disease (14.5%), and cancer 
(8.5%). All patients were APOE4 non-carriers or heterozygous APOE4 carriers (VAHS excludes APOE 
ε4 homozygotes). By the study date, 18.8% patients received LEC for ≤3 months, 18.8% for 3–6 
months, 44.4% for 7–12 months, and 18.0% for more than 1 year. After LEC initiation, 9.4% patients 
had ARIA, including 7.7% ARIA-E, 8.5% ARIA-H, 0.9% isolated ARIA-E ,1.7% isolated ARIA-H, and 4.3% 
symptomatic ARIA. Mean time to ARIA was 118.0±84.1 days (median=77 days). As of July 2025, ARIA-E 
was resolved in 4/9 cases and ARIA-H was generally stabilized. Infusions resumed in 3 cases. One 
emergency visit and no hospitalization were documented within 30 days of ARIA events. 

Conclusions: In this VAHS cohort, absolute risk of ARIA during the study observation period was 9.4% 
(11/117). Most ARIA events were mild or moderate and a minority were symptomatic. Data 
interpretation should consider modest sample size, variable treatment exposure, and incomplete 
observation of infusion pauses versus discontinuations. This study supports the feasibility of ARIA 
monitoring and management for LEC therapy in routine practice.

Aims: To investigate whether the pharmacodynamic (PD) profile induced by intravenous (IV) biperiden 
can be reversed by the acetylcholinesterase inhibitor donepezil, thereby validating the IV biperiden 
challenge model for proof-of-pharmacology studies with novel muscarinic acetylcholine receptor 
(mAChR) modulators. 

Methods: Double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomized, two-way crossover study in healthy elderly 
(≥65 to 80 years). Participants received 10 mg oral donepezil or placebo at the 0-hour timepoint, 
followed by a 1-hour IV infusion of 2.6 mg biperiden starting at the 3-hour timepoint. A validated test 
battery assessed pro- and anti-cholinergic effects up to 24 hours post-dose. Pharmacokinetic non-
compartmental analysis of both drugs was conducted. 

Results: 16 participants completed the study. A single dose of 10 mg donepezil improved adaptive 
tracking (1.69% [0.23–3.15], p=0.025) and N-back reaction times (one-back: −53.59 ms [−100.39, 
−6.79], p=0.026) at the 2.5-h timepoint (pre-biperiden), and reversed the PD effects induced by 2.6 mg 
IV biperiden at the 4-h timepoint. Reversals were observed in adaptive tracking (3.05% [1.56–4.53], 
p=0.0002), indicating enhanced sustained attention; N-back reaction times (one-back: −60.00 ms 
[−105.70, −14.30], p=0.012; zero-back: −65.71 ms [−101.33, −30.09], p=0.0006), suggesting improved 
processing speed; and immediate visual verbal learning (up to 1.9 [0.8–2.9], p=0.0016), indicating 
effects on learning. Additionally, compared to placebo, donepezil significantly reduced alpha, delta, 
and theta pharmaco-encephalography band amplitudes under both eyes-open and eyes-closed 
conditions. 

Conclusions: The model demonstrated low and acceptable intersubject (∼30–35%) and intrasubject 
(∼18–24%) variability in plasma Cmax and AUC0–last, further supporting its reliability for repeated-
measures study designs. These findings validate the 2.6 mg IV biperiden challenge model as a robust 
tool for proof-of-pharmacology studies of novel mAChR modulators in early-stage clinical 
development.

Aims: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is the most common cause of dementia. Agitation develops in 
approximately half of patients with AD, contributing to disease progression, poor quality of life, 
mortality risk, increased risk of institutionalization, and caregiver burden. With only 1 FDA-approved 
treatment for AD agitation, further treatment options are warranted. The M1/M4-preferring muscarinic 
agonist, xanomeline, previously showed antipsychotic activity in placebo-controlled trials in people 
with AD. Xanomeline combined with the peripherally restricted muscarinic receptor antagonist 
trospium chloride (X/T) is FDA approved to treat schizophrenia. In post hoc analyses of pooled data 
from the randomized, placebo-controlled EMERGENT trials, X/T showed improvement in agitation in 
participants with acute schizophrenia exacerbations. These data suggest that X/T may be effective in 
treating AD symptoms. Our aim is to evaluate the safety and efficacy of X/T for the treatment of 
agitation in AD. 

Methods: ADAGIO-1 (NCT07011732) and ADAGIO-2 (NCT07011745) are identical, ongoing, 14-week, 
phase 3, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group trials of participants aged 55-
90 years with AD diagnosis including biomarker confirmation of AD pathology and at least 2 weeks of 
agitation prior to screening. Agitation is defined by Neuropsychiatric Inventory (NPI)/NPI-Nursing 
Home and Clinical Global Impressions-Severity (CGI-S) scales scores greater or equal to 4 and by 
Cohen-Mansfield Agitation Inventory-International Psychogeriatric Association (CMAI-IPA) criteria at 
screening and baseline visits. 

Results: The trials are currently recruiting to enroll approximately 704 participants total. The primary 
endpoint is change from baseline to end of treatment in CMAI-IPA total score. Secondary outcome 
measures include change from baseline in CGI-S scale. Safety and additional efficacy measures will 
also be evaluated. 

Conclusions: X/T has the potential to be a new treatment for AD agitation based on muscarinic 
receptor agonism.

Aims: Tau protein oligomers and fibrillar aggregates exert neurotoxicity in Alzheimer’s disease (AD) 
and other tauopathies. Development of compounds that directly disassemble these Tau assemblies 
into harmless physiological Tau monomers will disrupt their self-replication and toxicity and will 
enable disease-modifying treatments for AD and other tauopathies. Here, we report the development 
of all-D-enantiomeric peptide ligands that bind monomeric full-length Tau with high affinity, thereby 
stabilizing the physiological intrinsically disordered structure and preventing initiation of aggregation 
as well as eliminating already existing aggregates by disassembling them into monomers in a 
thermodynamic mode of action (MoA). 

Methods: Mirror-image phage display, next generation sequencing (NGS), surface plasmon 
resonance (SPR), Thioflavin-T aggregation assay (ThT-assay), cell-viability assay, seeded Tau 
aggregation in cells, chloroalkane penetration assay (CAPA-assay), time-resolved fluorescence energy 
transfer (TR-FRET) 

Results: We introduce our drug development toolbox of selecting all-D-enantiomeric compounds 
targeting Tau and verifying their thermodynamic MoA. The compound TF2D-5a was identified by 
mirror-image phage display, NGS and rational design [1]. It shows binding in the nanomolar range 
characterized by SPR and reduced full-length Tau aggregation in a heparin-free seeded Thioflavin-T 
(ThT) assay. We demonstrate cell penetration by the CAPA-assay and validate TF2D-5a’s inhibitory 
effect in cells using the TauRD-CFP/YFP biosensor cell system. Another important tool is a TR-FRET 
assay for demonstrating ex vivo target engagement using postmortem human brain homogenate 
samples of AD patients. [1] Altendorf, T. et al., Int J Mol Sci 24, 2161 (2023). 

Conclusions: The present work provides promising results for the development of lead compounds 
with a thermodynamic MoA for the future treatment of AD and other tauopathies.
